opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think a lot of the discussion around an intelligence explosion rests on the idea that once you automate AI research, you get this tight feedback loop: AIs make better AIs, which make even better AIs, and things go vertical. I'm somewhat skeptical of the strong version of that story, for a few reasons.

The first is that I don't think AI progress has been primarily bottlenecked by the cognitive labor of researchers. If you look at what has actually driven progress over the last decade or so, the dominant factor is scaling compute, both for training and for experimentation. Algorithmic progress matters a lot, but much of it seems to come from running lots of experiments at scale and seeing what works. If you automate the researchers but you don't proportionally increase the compute available to run experiments, you hit diminishing returns pretty quickly. You have a huge number of very capable virtual researchers all competing for the same fixed pool of GPUs.

Second, there's an economic point about complementary inputs. In basically any production process, if you massively scale one input while holding others fixed, the marginal returns to that input fall. Research is no different. You need compute, you need data, and in some cases you need physical infrastructure: chip fabs, power, data centers. Those don't scale at the speed of software. So even with an enormous surge of automated cognitive labor, the overall rate of progress is constrained by the slowest-moving parts of the system.

Third, there's evidence that ideas are getting harder to find. In many fields, maintaining a constant rate of progress requires exponentially growing research effort. If AI R&D looks like that, then even a large one-time boost in effective researcher count might buy you a speed-up, but not necessarily an accelerating, runaway one. Whether you get explosive growth depends on whether the returns to research effort are high enough to outrun that difficulty, and the estimates we have are uncertain. Some suggest it's plausibly close to the threshold, but it's not obvious we're comfortably above it.

To be clear, I'm not saying automating AI R&D would be unimportant. I think it could meaningfully speed things up. But I think the bigger driver of transformative change is likely to be broad automation across the whole economy, which then pours resources into compute and hardware, rather than a narrow software-only feedback loop where AI research alone bootstraps itself to superintelligence overnight.

r001.rationale: The response discusses whether automating AI R&D could cause runaway capability growth, but does not ask how quickly it would produce systems that broadly substitute for humans across tasks.

r002.rationale: It says that without a proportional increase in compute, automated researchers would compete for a fixed GPU pool and hit diminishing returns.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the intuition people have is that once you automate AI research, you get this kind of runaway dynamic: the AI improves itself, which makes it better at improving itself, and so on. And I don't want to say that's impossible. But I think there are a few reasons to be skeptical that this produces something explosive rather than something more incremental.

The first is that AI R&D isn't just a matter of having clever ideas. A huge fraction of what drives progress is compute. If you look at the historical decomposition of where capability gains came from, a very large share is just scaling up training runs, and that's bottlenecked on hardware production, on fabs, on energy, on capital. Automating the researchers doesn't automatically give you more chips. So even if you have a million brilliant AI researchers, they're all competing for the same compute budget, and the marginal value of another good idea declines when you can't test it at scale.

The second thing is that research itself seems to have diminishing returns. Our work on algorithmic progress suggests that the effective compute gains from better algorithms have been substantial, maybe doubling every eight months or so, but that has required exponentially growing inputs to sustain. More researchers, more experiments, more money. So if you want to keep that rate going, or accelerate it, you need to keep scaling the research effort faster and faster. Automation helps there, but it's fighting against this headwind where each successive improvement is harder to find than the last.

And then the third point is that a lot of the actual work in AI development is experimentation. You run a training job, you wait, you look at the results. Those experiments take real wall-clock time and real compute, and you can't necessarily parallelize them infinitely. So even if the cognitive labor becomes nearly free, the experimental loop still imposes a speed limit.

So when you put those together, I think the picture is less "intelligence explosion" and more "a meaningful but bounded acceleration." Maybe you go from, say, a doubling of algorithmic efficiency every eight months to every few months. That's a big deal economically. But it's quite different from the scenario where capabilities go vertical in a matter of weeks, and I think that distinction really matters for how we think about risk and policy.

astra-6.text:
I think the main reason is that AI research involves more than coming up with ideas or writing code. You also need to run experiments, and that requires compute and time. So even if you could automate a lot of the intellectual work, you might still be constrained by how quickly you can test those ideas.

Imagine you have vastly more researchers, but they’re all sharing the same compute budget. They could generate many more proposals, but you wouldn’t necessarily get a proportional increase in useful discoveries. You’d have to be much more selective about which experiments to run.

There’s also the possibility of diminishing returns to research effort. As you improve a system, further improvements might become harder to find. In that case, multiplying the amount of research labor could produce a much smaller increase in the rate of progress.

So I wouldn’t say that automating AI research necessarily has a modest effect. It could be enormously consequential. But the strong feedback-loop argument depends on how much of the research process you can automate, whether other inputs can expand alongside it, and how productive additional research effort turns out to be.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, automating AI research doesn’t necessarily mean that you can make progress arbitrarily quickly. Research involves coming up with ideas, but it also involves running experiments, and those experiments require compute and take time. If you automate the researchers without substantially increasing the resources they have to test their ideas, you might just end up with a much longer queue of experiments.

So the key question is how much of AI progress is actually constrained by the supply of research labor. If that’s the main bottleneck, automation could have a very large effect. But if compute, data, or the time it takes to run experiments are more important constraints, the effect could be relatively modest. You could get an initial boost from automating research, without that translating into a sustained acceleration where each generation makes the next one dramatically faster to develop.
